claim: NRL is a Maf-family basic motif leucine zipper (bZIP) transcription factor.
source: The Maf-family basic motif leucine zipper (bZIP) transcription factor neural retina leucine (NRL) determines rod photoreceptor cell fate as its loss leads to retina with only cone photoreceptors (Mears et al., 2001)
evidence: This is stated directly in the text with citation to prior work.

claim: Loss of NRL leads to retina with only cone photoreceptors.
source: The Maf-family basic motif leucine zipper (bZIP) transcription factor neural retina leucine (NRL) determines rod photoreceptor cell fate as its loss leads to retina with only cone photoreceptors (Mears et al., 2001)
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citation to Mears et al., 2001.

claim: Ectopic expression of NRL in developing cones results in generation of rods.
source: whereas ectopic expression of NRL in developing cones results in generation of rods (Oh et al., 2007)
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citation to Oh et al., 2007.

claim: Continued expression of NRL is essential for maintaining rod function.
source: Continued expression of NRL is essential for maintaining rod function (Yu et al., 2017)
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citation to Yu et al., 2017.

claim: Mutations affecting NRL activity are associated with retinopathies.
source: and mutations affecting NRL activity are associated with retinopathies (Bessant et al., 1999; Nishiguchi et al., 2004; Kanda et al., 2007; El-Asrag et al., 2022)
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by multiple citations.

claim: NRL regulates precise transcriptional output of thousands of genes.
source: NRL establishes rod cell identity and function by regulating precise transcriptional output of thousands of genes (Hao et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2016; Liang et al., 2022)
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: NRL collaborates with cone rod homeobox (CRX) to regulate gene expression.
source: NRL establishes rod cell identity and function by regulating precise transcriptional output of thousands of genes (Hao et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2016; Liang et al., 2022) in collaboration with cone rod homeobox (CRX) (Mitton et al., 2000; Hennig et al., 2008; Corbo et al., 2010)
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citations.

claim: Transcriptional activation synergy was observed in rhodopsin regulation between NRL and NonO/p54nrb.
source: This prediction was strengthened by transcriptional activation synergy observed in rhodopsin regulation between NRL and NonO/p54nrb (Yadav et al., 2014)
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citation to Yadav et al., 2014.

claim: NonO is a ubiquitous nuclear paraspeckle protein that binds to DNA, RNA as well as proteins.
source: NonO, a ubiquitous nuclear paraspeckle protein, binds to DNA, RNA as well as proteins, and regulates distinct cellular events including the coupling of the circadian clock to cell cycle and transcription to splicing (Fox and Lamond, 2010; Kowalska et al., 2013; Feng et al., 2020)
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citations.

claim: RBPs constitute over 40% of NRL interactors identified in GST-NRL pull-down experiments.
source: RBPs represented over 40% of NRL interactors in this set (12/28) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: 28 proteins were significantly enriched (>twofold, p < 0.05) compared to control samples in three independent GST-NRL pull-down experiments.
source: We identified 28 proteins that were significantly enriched (>twofold, p < 0.05) compared to control samples in three independent GST-NRL pull-down experiments (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Interaction of NRL with DHX9, HNRNPU, or HNRNPUl1 remained robust after incubation with Benzonase.
source: Notably, interaction of NRL with DHX9, HNRNPU, or HNRNPUl1 remained robust even after incubation of the nuclear lysate with Benzonase, a promiscuous nuclease that digests all nucleic acid species, whereas HNRNPA1, HNRNPM, and HNRPA2B1 were not or barely pulled down after treatment, indicating a requirement of nucleic acids for the latter set of interactions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: HNRNPA1, HNRNPM, and HNRPA2B1 interactions with NRL require nucleic acids.
source: Notably, interaction of NRL with DHX9, HNRNPU, or HNRNPUl1 remained robust even after incubation of the nuclear lysate with Benzonase, a promiscuous nuclease that digests all nucleic acid species, whereas HNRNPA1, HNRNPM, and HNRPA2B1 were not or barely pulled down after treatment, indicating a requirement of nucleic acids for the latter set of interactions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Immunoprecipitation using anti-NRL antibody of NRL-enriched high molecular mass fractions from bovine retina identified several RBP interactors.
source: Independently and concurrently, immunoprecipitation using anti-NRL antibody of NRL-enriched high molecular mass fractions from the bovine retina, followed by mass spectrometry analysis, identified several RBP interactors in addition to known interacting proteins such as CRX, NR2E3, and NonO/p54nrb (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Supplementary file 2.

claim: The most enriched proteins in bovine retina NRL immunoprecipitation included DHX9, HRRNPU, and HNRNPM.
source: Notably, the most enriched proteins included DHX9, HRRNPU, and HNRNPM.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text.

claim: 'mRNA-binding' was the top 4% highest enriched gene ontology term in bovine and mouse pull downs.
source: Out of the 786 and 1491 proteins identified in bovine and mouse pull downs, respectively (Supplementary file 2), 'mRNA-binding' was the top 4% highest enriched gene ontology term (adjusted p-value = 1.27E−53 and 2.1E−21, respectively).
evidence: This is directly stated with statistical support.

claim: 30 RBPs were identified in at least two assays for NRL interaction.
source: Notably, 30 of these proteins were identified in at least two assays, and two of these, DHX9 and HNRNPM, in three assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: DHX9 and HNRNPM were identified in three out of four NRL interaction assays.
source: Notably, 30 of these proteins were identified in at least two assays, and two of these, DHX9 and HNRNPM, in three assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PRPF8 and SNRNP200 have been implicated in photoreceptor degeneration.
source: Notably, two of the RBPs (PRPF8 and SNRNP200) Escher et al., 2018 have been implicated in photoreceptor degeneration and harbor substantial interactions in this subnetwork (Figure 1E, black rectangle).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to Escher et al., 2018.

claim: DHX9, DDX5, DDX17, and DDX3X are RNA helicases with prominent roles in the regulation of R-loops.
source: We also noted that some RBPs in the network (DHX9, DDX5, DDX17, and DDX3X) are RNA helicases with prominent roles in the regulation of R-loops, which are non-B DNA structures comprising of RNA-DNA hybrids and displaced single-stranded DNA with multiple regulatory roles in transcription (Kim and Wang, 2021).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to Kim and Wang, 2021.

claim: 50% of NRL-interacting RBPs were identified in the high-confidence R-loop protein group.
source: Strikingly, 50% of NRL-interacting RBPs were also identified in this high-confidence R-loop protein group indicating a high enrichment of R-loop-associated RBPs among NRL interactors (Fisher's exact test p = 2E−13) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is directly stated with statistical support (Fisher's exact test p = 2E−13).

claim: DHX9 localizes to the rod nuclear periphery, which corresponds to the euchromatin compartment of murine rods.
source: Notably, immunofluorescence of mouse retina reveals the localization of DHX9 and DDX5 in the rod nuclear periphery, which corresponds to the euchromatin compartment of murine rods (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: DDX5 localizes to the rod nuclear periphery, which corresponds to the euchromatin compartment of murine rods.
source: Notably, immunofluorescence of mouse retina reveals the localization of DHX9 and DDX5 in the rod nuclear periphery, which corresponds to the euchromatin compartment of murine rods (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: DHX9 is expressed in all nuclei of mouse retina.
source: In mouse retina, DHX9 is observed in all nuclei (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: NRL and DHX9 show robust positive interaction signal in the outer nuclear layer of mouse retina by PLA.
source: PLAs using anti-NRL and DHX9 antibodies show robust positive interaction signal in the outer nuclear layer (Figure 2B) where NRL is normally expressed (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: No PLA signal above background is detectable for NRL-DHX9 interaction in Nrl KO retina.
source: In contrast, no signal above background is detectable when PLA is performed in Nrl KO retina (Figure 2B), suggesting the specificity of PLA signals, even though DHX9 is still expressed throughout the KO retina nuclei (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: DDX5 shows widespread expression throughout the retina.
source: DDX5 also shows widespread expression throughout the retina (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: DDX5 displays a lower yet specific interaction signal with NRL in the outer nuclear layer by PLA.
source: DDX5 also shows widespread expression throughout the retina (Figure 2C) but displays a lower yet specific interaction signal with NRL in the outer nuclear layer by PLA (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 2D.

claim: NRL-DDX5 PLA signal is absent in Nrl KO retina.
source: This signal is absent in Nrl KO retina (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 2D.

claim: DHX9 and DDX5 are detected in all nuclear layers of the human retina.
source: Similar to mouse retina, DHX9 and DDX5 are detected in all nuclear layers of the human retina whereas NRL is present only in the outer nuclear layer of photoreceptors (Figure 2E, G).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figures 2E and 2G.

claim: NRL is present only in the outer nuclear layer of photoreceptors in human retina.
source: Similar to mouse retina, DHX9 and DDX5 are detected in all nuclear layers of the human retina whereas NRL is present only in the outer nuclear layer of photoreceptors (Figure 2E, G).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figures 2E and 2G.

claim: NRL–DHX9 PLA signal is clearly detected in the outer nuclear layer of the human retina.
source: Consistent with the results in mouse, NRL–DHX9 PLA signal is clearly detected in the outer nuclear layer of the human retina (Figure 2F), indicating a robust and reproducible interaction between NRL and DHX9.
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 2F.

claim: NRL-DDX5 PLA signals do not seem to be above negative control in human retina.
source: However, NRL-DDX5 PLA signals do not seem to be above negative control (Figure 2H, I).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figures 2H and 2I.

claim: In HEK293 cells overexpressing human NRL, PLA signals are robust for both DHX9 and DDX5 throughout the nuclear compartment.
source: Interestingly, in HEK293 cells overexpressing human NRL, PLA signals are robust for both DHX9 and DDX5 throughout the nuclear compartment (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 2J.

claim: DHX9 and HNRNPU PLA signals are enriched mostly in the nuclear periphery in HEK293 cells.
source: DHX9 and HNRNPU serve as a positive control for PLA and are enriched mostly in the nuclear periphery (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 2J.

claim: Over 50% of RBP genes possess NRL ChIP-Seq peaks.
source: Interestingly, over 50% of RBP genes possess NRL ChIP-Seq peaks and almost 25% harbor super enhancers (SEs) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Almost 25% of RBP genes harbor super enhancers.
source: Interestingly, over 50% of RBP genes possess NRL ChIP-Seq peaks and almost 25% harbor super enhancers (SEs) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: NRL binds to super enhancer regions at DDX5, HNRNPU, DDX3X, and THRAP3 genes.
source: Figure 3—figure supplement 1A shows a few examples of NRL binding to super enhancers regions at DDX5, HNRNPU, DDX3X, and THRAP3 genes.
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: NRL-binding peaks are identified in both human and mouse DHX9 promoter regions.
source: We then focused on the DHX9 locus and could identify NRL-binding peaks in both human and mouse promoter regions (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figures 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Lower levels of Dhx9 transcripts are observed in Nrl KO photoreceptors.
source: In concordance, we observe lower levels of Dhx9 transcripts in Nrl KO photoreceptors (Kim et al., 2016; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Kim et al., 2016 and Figure 3C.

claim: A canonical NRL-binding site is identified at the human DHX9 promoter that is partially conserved in mouse.
source: A search of NRL ChIP-Seq peaks (Hao et al., 2012) at the human DHX9 promoter identified a canonical NRL-binding site that is partially conserved in mouse, in concordance with NRL Cut&Run data from mouse retina (Liang et al., 2022; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations and reference to Figure 3D.

claim: Bovine retina nuclear proteins bind to a probe containing the NRL-binding site at the DHX9 promoter.
source: Using a probe containing this sequence, we demonstrate binding of bovine retina nuclear proteins by electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSAs) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: Probes with mutations in and around the putative NRL-binding site were not able to compete with the wild-type probe for binding.
source: Although we did not directly measure NRL binding to this sequence, probes with mutations in and around the putative NRL-binding site were not able to compete with the wild-type probe for binding (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 3E.

claim: The interaction of DHX9 and NRL is enhanced upon treatment of lysates with RNase A in HEK293 cells overexpressing NRL.
source: In HEK293 cells overexpressing NRL, the interaction of DHX9 and NRL is enhanced upon treatment of lysates with RNase A (Figure 4A, C), indicating a negative regulation by RNA.
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figures 4A and 4C.

claim: RNA negatively regulates the interaction between NRL and DHX9.
source: In HEK293 cells overexpressing NRL, the interaction of DHX9 and NRL is enhanced upon treatment of lysates with RNase A (Figure 4A, C), indicating a negative regulation by RNA.
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figures 4A and 4C.

claim: Treatment with RNase H reduced NRL's interaction with both DHX9 and DDX5.
source: On the other hand, treatment with RNase H, which digests RNA only in the DNA:RNA hybrid context, reduced NRL's interaction with both DHX9 and DDX5 suggesting a positive impact of DNA:RNA hybrids (Figure 4A, C).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figures 4A and 4C.

claim: DNA:RNA hybrids positively impact NRL's interaction with DHX9 and DDX5.
source: On the other hand, treatment with RNase H, which digests RNA only in the DNA:RNA hybrid context, reduced NRL's interaction with both DHX9 and DDX5 suggesting a positive impact of DNA:RNA hybrids (Figure 4A, C).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figures 4A and 4C.

claim: Pull down of DHX9 and DDX5 from bovine retina extract with endogenous NRL was decreased upon removal of DNA:RNA hybrids.
source: Pull down of DHX9 and DDX5 from bovine retina extract with endogenous NRL was not altered by RNase A treatment but was decreased upon removal of DNA:RNA hybrids (Figure 4E, G), suggesting a role of R-loops in regulating NRL interactions.
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figures 4E and 4G.

claim: R-loops play a role in regulating NRL interactions.
source: Pull down of DHX9 and DDX5 from bovine retina extract with endogenous NRL was not altered by RNase A treatment but was decreased upon removal of DNA:RNA hybrids (Figure 4E, G), suggesting a role of R-loops in regulating NRL interactions.
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figures 4E and 4G.

claim: The binding between DHX9 and DDX5 was decreased when RNase A was present in bovine retina.
source: Notably, the binding between DHX9 and DDX5 was decreased when RNase A was present (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), indicating a positive regulatory role of RNA in the retina.
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RNA plays a positive regulatory role in DHX9-DDX5 binding in the retina.
source: Notably, the binding between DHX9 and DDX5 was decreased when RNase A was present (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), indicating a positive regulatory role of RNA in the retina.
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: DNA did not influence NRL interactions as evidenced by treatments of lysates with DNase I.
source: DNA did not influence NRL interactions as evidenced by treatments of lysates with DNase I, which has only 1% activity on DNA:RNA hybrids (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figures 4A–D.

claim: NRL is enriched in R-loops along with DHX9 after incubation with mouse retinal nuclear lysates.
source: After incubations with mouse retinal nuclear lysates, NRL is enriched in R-loops along with DHX9 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: DDX5 does not appear to bind to retinal R-loops.
source: However, DDX5 does not appear to bind to retinal R-loops, suggesting that DDX5 association with R-loops is weaker, transient, or more regulated in the retina, and in agreement with co-IP findings from RNase H-treated bovine retina lysates.
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: Overexpression of wild-type RNase H1 reduces R-loop levels in HEK293 cells.
source: We then overexpressed GFP-tagged RNase H1 in HEK293 cells to reduce the R-loop levels, as shown previously (Crossley et al., 2023)
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to Crossley et al., 2023.

claim: A reduction in the number of cells displaying NRL–DHX9 nuclear PLA signals is detected in cells with wild-type nuclear RNase H1 compared to cells with catalytically inactive RNase H1.
source: We detect a reduction in the number of cells displaying NRL–DHX9 nuclear PLA signals in cells that also harbor wild-type nuclear RNase H1 as compared to the cells having catalytically inactive version of RNase H1 (GFP-dHR) (Figure 5B and D).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figures 5B and 5D.

claim: A small percentage of cells with PLA signals enriched in subnuclear compartments is observed, especially in cells with wild-type RNase H1.
source: In addition, we observe a small percentage of cells with PLA signals enriched in subnuclear compartments, especially in cells with wild-type RNase H1 (Figure 5B, E, arrows).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figures 5B and 5E.

claim: The localization of NRL or DHX9 is not influenced by the expression of RNase H1.
source: Notably, the localization of NRL or DHX9 is not influenced by the expression of RNase H1 (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: NRL and DHX9 interaction in the nucleoplasm is favored by R-loops.
source: Thus, NRL and DHX9 interaction in the nucleoplasm is favored by R-loops, and R-loops appear to influence the stabilization and localization of NRL–DHX9 complexes.
evidence: This is directly stated as a conclusion from the data.

claim: R-loops appear to influence the stabilization and localization of NRL–DHX9 complexes.
source: Thus, NRL and DHX9 interaction in the nucleoplasm is favored by R-loops, and R-loops appear to influence the stabilization and localization of NRL–DHX9 complexes.
evidence: This is directly stated as a conclusion from the data.

claim: R-loop levels increase with postnatal retinal maturation.
source: Quantification of R-loop levels using the S9.6 antibody reveals an increase in R-loops with postnatal retinal maturation (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 6A.

claim: Total R-loop levels increase in the Nrl KO retina.
source: Total R-loop levels increase in the Nrl KO retina, indicating a role of R-loops in controlling cell type-specific gene expression and/or the role of NRL in regulating R-loop levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: 4677 R-loops were identified in ssDRIP-Seq data that were absent in RNase H-treated samples.
source: We identified 4677 R-loops in our ssDRIP-Seq data that were absent in RNase H-treated samples (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 2B, C.

claim: 3352 R-loops were identified as unstranded (without strand specificity).
source: Our analysis uncovered 3352 loops without any strand specificity (hereafter referred as unstranded) and 1328 strand-specific R-loops (hereafter referred as stranded).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text.

claim: 1328 R-loops were identified as stranded (strand-specific).
source: Our analysis uncovered 3352 loops without any strand specificity (hereafter referred as unstranded) and 1328 strand-specific R-loops (hereafter referred as stranded).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text.

claim: Stranded R-loops are enriched at pseudogenes.
source: Intriguingly, stranded R-loops are also enriched at pseudogenes, whereas unstranded R-loops are only enriched at intergenic regions (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 6C.

claim: Unstranded R-loops are only enriched at intergenic regions.
source: Intriguingly, stranded R-loops are also enriched at pseudogenes, whereas unstranded R-loops are only enriched at intergenic regions (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 6C.

claim: Stranded R-loops are preferentially observed around the transcription start site (TSS).
source: In agreement, stranded R-loops are preferentially observed around the transcription start site (TSS), but unstranded R-loops are further downstream of the transcription termination site (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Unstranded R-loops are further downstream of the transcription termination site.
source: In agreement, stranded R-loops are preferentially observed around the transcription start site (TSS), but unstranded R-loops are further downstream of the transcription termination site (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Stranded R-loops are enriched at neuronal genes associated with synapse function.
source: We found that stranded R-loops were particularly enriched at neuronal genes associated with synapse function (Figure 6D)
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 6D.

claim: Unstranded R-loops are enriched at genes associated with G-protein-coupled receptor signaling.
source: and unstranded R-loops were also enriched at genes associated with G-protein-coupled receptor signaling (Figure 6—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 2F.

claim: R-loops were identified in 20 genes involved in retinal disease including Ush2a, Pcdh15, and Abcc6.
source: In addition, R-loops were identified in 20 genes involved in retinal disease including Ush2a, Pcdh15, and Abcc6 (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Supplementary file 4.

claim: Stranded R-loops harbor histone marks associated with active transcription including H3K36me3, H3K4me2, and H3k4me3.
source: We observed that stranded and unstranded R-loops displayed differences in their epigenetic signatures. Stranded R-loops harbor histone marks associated with active transcription including H3K36me3, H3K4me2, and H3k4me3.
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 6E.

claim: Unstranded R-loops were only enriched with H3K9me3, associated with heterochromatin.
source: However, unstranded R-loops were only enriched with H3K9me3, associated with heterochromatin (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 6E.

claim: NRL is enriched at both stranded and unstranded R-loops.
source: Next, we investigated whether NRL binds to R-loops and found that NRL is enriched at both stranded an unstranded R-loops, suggesting a strong association of NRL to R-loops regardless of the epigenetic context (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 7A.

claim: BRD4, CTCF, and Pol II were primarily associated with stranded R-loops.
source: Notably, other chromatin-binding factors such as BRD4, CTCF, and Pol II were primarily associated with stranded R-loops.
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 7A.

claim: NRL binding was associated with a higher proportion of R-loops at low and high expression genes.
source: In addition, NRL binding was associated with a higher proportion of R-loops at low and high expression genes (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: NRL target genes have an enrichment of stranded R-loops at the promoter/TSS and unstranded R-loops on the gene body compared to all genes annotated in Ensembl.
source: Overall, NRL target genes have an enrichment of stranded R-loops at the promoter/TSS and unstranded R-loops on the gene body compared to all genes annotated in Ensembl (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Genes without any R-loop are shorter than those overlapping with R-loops, independently of their expression level.
source: Curiously, the genes without any R-loop are shorter than those overlapping with R-loops, independently of their expression level (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 7D.

claim: In genes showing low to mid-level expression, a concomitant formation of stranded and unstranded R-loops is associated with longer genes compared to the genes with stranded only or unstranded only R-loops.
source: In genes showing low to mid-level expression, a concomitant formation of stranded and unstranded R-loops is associated with longer genes compared to the genes with stranded only or unstranded only R-loops (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is directly stated with reference to Figure 7D.

claim: R-loops are formed during transcription and play key roles in transcriptional initiation, elongation, and termination.
source: Most R-loops are formed during transcription and play key roles in transcriptional initiation, elongation, and termination.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text.

claim: R-loops are sufficient to initiate transcription of antisense lncRNA from enhancers and other genomic regions.
source: R-loops are reportedly sufficient to initiate transcription of antisense lncRNA from enhancers and other genomic regions (Tan-Wong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to Tan-Wong et al., 2019.

claim: R-loops contribute to Pol II pausing at promoters and in gene bodies.
source: R-loops also contribute to Pol II pausing at promoters and in gene bodies, thereby influencing transcriptional outputs (Tous and Aguilera, 2007).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to Tous and Aguilera, 2007.

claim: Accumulation of R-loops at polyadenylation-dependent termination regions can cause transcriptional termination.
source: Accumulation of R-loops at polyadenylation-dependent termination regions (Sanz et al., 2016) and R-loop-prone sequences downstream from poly A cleavage sites can cause transcriptional termination (Skourti-Stathaki et al., 2011).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations to Sanz et al., 2016 and Skourti-Stathaki et al., 2011.

claim: R-loops may indirectly control gene expression by influencing chromatin structure and the epigenome.
source: Additionally, R-loops may indirectly control gene expression by influencing chromatin structure and the epigenome (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to Chen et al., 2015.

claim: The greater likelihood of neuronal genes to harbor R-loops may be because of their larger gene size.
source: The greater likelihood of neuronal genes to harbor R-loops may also be because of their larger gene size (Gabel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to Gabel et al., 2015.

claim: R-loops may contribute to regulation of long neural genes as is the case for DNA damage.
source: R-loops may also contribute to regulation of long neural genes as is the case for DNA damage (Wei et al., 2016).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to Wei et al., 2016.

claim: Bidirectional transcription is associated with the formation of repressive genomic regions.
source: Our results indicate that unstranded R-loops (containing RNA:DNA hybrids on both strands) are enriched in intergenic regions and occur downstream of genes, overlapping the repressive mark H3K9me3. This observation suggests that bidirectional transcription is associated with the formation of repressive genomic regions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that unstranded R-loops overlap with H3K9me3.

claim: R-loops are involved in maintenance of heterochromatin and telomers.
source: Indeed, R-loops are also reported to be involved in maintenance of heterochromatin and telomers (Pfeiffer et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations to Pfeiffer et al., 2013 and Xu et al., 2017.

claim: R-loops can induce antisense transcription at gene termination sequences, leading to the generation of double-stranded RNA and recruitment of G9a histone methyltransferase.
source: For example, R-loops can induce antisense transcription at gene termination sequences, leading to the generation of double-stranded RNA and recruitment of G9a histone methyltransferase (Skourti-Stathaki et al., 2014).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to Skourti-Stathaki et al., 2014.

claim: Bidirectional transcription termination by Pol II offers a potential mechanism of termination at convergent genes.
source: Bidirectional transcription termination by Pol II also offers a potential mechanism of termination at convergent genes (Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to Wang et al., 2023.

claim: R-loops localizing near H3K9me3 sites are associated with regulation of long genes.
source: R-loops localizing near H3K9me3 sites are shown to be associated with regulation of long genes (Manzo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is directly stated with citation to Manzo et al., 2018.

claim: NRL genomic occupancy overlaps with unstranded R-loops at the gene body, suggesting a functional link that may be unrelated to transcriptional initiation.
